question: The impact of nuclear tests on people and the environment remains a major concern for the populations of French Polynesia, and is an issue which requires continued attention at European level.

The situation in French Polynesia after the 193 nuclear tests (including four atmospheric tests) carried out by France between 1960 and 1996 raises urgent questions about public health and the environment, as well as reparations and compensation for victims.

It is essential to fully understand the impact of these tests on Polynesian society, including the ecological, climate, health, economic, social and environmental impacts. Concerns persist about the transparency of information on radiation doses received by populations at the time of testing, as well as on the extent of dispersion of radioactive particles.

In view of these concerns, is the Commission planning to set up a committee of inquiry to assess the impact of nuclear tests in French Polynesia? Such an initiative should include examining the initial decisions on site selection and the state of the art before and after the tests, as well as action taken to compensate victims and repair the environmental damage.
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (24.6.2024) The Euratom Treaty seeks to protect its citizens against the dangers of increased exposure to ionising radiation which may be harmful to human health.

However, according to a judgement of the Court of Justice of the European Union in 2006, the use of nuclear energy for military purposes falls outside the scope of all the provisions of the Euratom Treaty1 and its secondary legislation2. Therefore, the Commission has no competence, under the Euratom Treaty, to set up a committee of inquiry to assess the impact of nuclear tests in French Polynesia.

The Commission is, however, closely monitoring the application of the highest standards of protection of the public and the environment against the effects of ionising radiation. The Commission also monitors and follows-up on the data resulting from the radiation monitoring in the environment put in place by the French authorities in French Polynesia.

France has transposed the Basic Safety Standards Directive3 into its national legislation and is thus applying these standards to ensure appropriate protection of all people living in French territories, including those in French Polynesia. This includes the obligation to ensure that an appropriate environmental monitoring programme is in place (Article 72 of the Directive).

Moreover, according to Article 35 of the Euratom Treaty, each Member State shall establish the facilities necessary to carry out continuous monitoring of the level of radioactivity in the air, water and soil and to ensure compliance with the basic standards. The Commission has the right to access such facilities and verify their operation and efficiency.
